Compared with a simple read of the opening line, the full FOMC statement is more balanced: it notes “further progress” toward 2 percent inflation and risks “moving into better balance,” but pairs that with a high-for-long stance (holding the 5.25–5.50% target range, continuing QT, and requiring “greater confidence” before cutting). In standard monetary policy models and practice, this is consistent with rule-like behavior: with inflation still above target and the output gap uncertain, a Taylor-rule framework typically prescribes keeping the policy rate restrictive until the inflation gap closes (Federal Reserve behavior resembling a Taylor rule; Lubik and Schorfheide highlight the need for a sufficiently strong inflation response to avoid indeterminacy). The emphasis on expectations management and conditional forward guidance aligns with the literature on interest-rate rules as commitment devices (Woodford) and on credibility in inflation targeting. The caution against premature easing also reflects the real-time data pitfalls stressed by Orphanides. QT and administered rates (IORB, ON RRP) indicate the Fed is using its floor-system tools to transmit the stance and influence the term structure (Cochrane and Piazzesi on the yield curve). Overall, the tone is modestly positive relative to prior risk assessments but tempered by the explicit high-for-long posture.
